question: How significant was Rosa Parks, and why?
status: A–F are new factual teaching summaries, written in 2026. No old text, speech, testimony or picture is copied. They describe the past; our scores are reasoned views about it.

evidence_cards.title: Work before the bus protest
evidence_cards.body: In 1943, Rosa Parks became secretary of a local civil rights group. She helped record unfair treatment and worked for equal rights. Her work began years before her bus arrest.
evidence_cards.limit: This shows earlier work, not a measure of all the change she caused.

evidence_cards.title: A refusal and arrest
evidence_cards.body: In Montgomery, racist bus rules kept Black and White people apart. On 1 December 1955, Parks refused to give up her seat. Police arrested her. Local groups then called for a bus boycott on 5 December.
evidence_cards.limit: Her action helped prompt the boycott. Organisers and earlier campaigns also mattered.

evidence_cards.title: A protest kept going by many
evidence_cards.body: Many Black residents stayed off Montgomery buses. People walked, shared rides and raised funds. Local organisers helped the protest last. Parks’s action mattered within this joint work. One person could not keep it going alone.
evidence_cards.limit: The shared work limits a claim that Parks alone won change.

evidence_cards.title: A separate case changed bus law
evidence_cards.body: The court case Browder v. Gayle challenged bus segregation. Parks was not one of its plaintiffs. Judges ruled against the bus rules. After the court order arrived, the boycott ended. People returned to integrated buses on 21 December 1956.
evidence_cards.limit: Bus law changed through legal action too. Racism did not end.

evidence_cards.title: Work continued in Detroit
evidence_cards.body: Parks later lived in Detroit. From 1965 to 1988 she worked in a member of Congress’s local office. She helped people with their needs and kept working for civil rights. Her public work reached beyond one bus journey.
evidence_cards.limit: A job and years of work alone do not measure every result.

evidence_cards.title: Public honours and remembrance
evidence_cards.body: Parks received a gold medal from Congress in 1999. A statue of her was placed in the US Capitol in 2013, after her death in 2005. These are signs of wide public remembrance.
evidence_cards.limit: Public honours show recognition. They do not tell us what every person knows or prove she acted alone.

criteria.title: Changed things at the time
criteria.meaning: Did the person help change events or lives then? How far?
criteria.caution: Separate her part from the work of others.

criteria.title: Still matters now
criteria.meaning: What can this history help us think about today? Why?
criteria.caution: A useful lesson now is a reasoned link, not proof she caused every later change.

criteria.title: Remembered by many
criteria.meaning: Is there evidence of wide public remembrance? What kind?
criteria.caution: Public honours show remembrance. They do not prove every claim about impact.

criteria.title: Revealed something
criteria.meaning: What does her story show about unfair rules or how change happens?
criteria.caution: Use a fact to support what it shows. Keep the shared work in view.

scale: The cards give no clear support for this claim.
Some support, but narrow or limited.
Clear support, with a limit to explain.
Strong support, with a limit still kept in view.
significance_evaluation.weighting: The four criteria have equal weight for this teaching task. That is a classroom choice, not a universal historical rule.
significance_evaluation.judgement_status: Scores are reasoned judgements about the supplied evidence, not objective measurements or scores of a person’s worth. Different scores are acceptable when the evidence, reason and limit support them.
significance_evaluation.grid_requirement: Each pupil records four scores, one card code and reason for each, and a limit to each judgement; then totals out of 12 and writes a reasoned paragraph.
significance_evaluation.limit: Parks contributed to collective change. Organisers, many residents and a separate court case also mattered. Bus desegregation did not end racism. Public honours demonstrate remembrance; fame alone does not establish every kind of significance.

grid_rows: C1 Changed things at the time

model.status: Original teacher-written judgement; no historical quotation, testimony, image or footage.
model.text: For C3, remembered by many, I might give 3 out of 3. Card F lists national honours and a statue in the US Capitol. These show wide public recognition. But they do not tell us what every person knows. This is one part of her significance. It does not prove she caused all change alone.
